clue.text: Gravy goodness in remains of food

parts.note: both are mild exclamations of surprise

explanation.surface: A cook praises the nourishing value of gravy made from leftovers.
explanation.walkthrough: Gravy and goodness both look like kitchen nouns, but one is slang for cash and the other an exclamation, as in 'Crumbs!'.
explanation.definitionFit: Breadcrumbs are the small bits left over from a loaf.

clue.text: Approach rugby union joke the wrong way

indicators.note: a joke read the wrong way round is read backwards

explanation.surface: Someone tackles a rugby joke from the wrong angle.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the joke is turned round; RU stays as it is.
explanation.definitionFit: The run-up is the approach a bowler or jumper makes before the act.

clue.text: Put out drink for JFK, say?

parts.note: to put out a programme is to air it

explanation.surface: Someone sets out a drink for President Kennedy.
explanation.walkthrough: JFK looks like the president, but the question mark flags an example: it is New York's airport named after him.
explanation.definitionFit: JFK is an airport in New York, so an example of one.

clue.text: Ring cleric when upset

indicators.note: an upset cleric is knocked out of order

explanation.surface: You phone a vicar whenever he is distressed.
explanation.walkthrough: Ring looks like a verb, to telephone, but it is the noun: a round shape.
explanation.definitionFit: Ring and circle are plain synonyms for a round band or shape; the surface makes ring the telephone verb.

clue.text: Outsider, criminal rounded on leader in gymkhana

indicators.note: criminal letters are crooked, out of their proper order
the leader of gymkhana is its first letter

explanation.surface: At a horse show, a crook turns on the leading rider.
explanation.walkthrough: Rounded on reads as 'turned on', but rounded is the fodder and on means G comes after it.
explanation.definitionFit: An outsider in a contest is the underdog, not expected to win.

clue.text: Cry buckets — thick tissue!

definitions.meaning: the thick fat layer of whales and seals

explanation.walkthrough: Blubber is a verb, to weep noisily, and a noun, the thick fat of whales; 'tissue' tempts you towards a paper hanky for the tears.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the verb, to sob noisily; the other the noun, the thick fatty layer under a whale's skin.

clue.text: Principal in Canada, one entering Toronto, isn't bothered — twisted individual?

indicators.note: the principal, or first, letter of Canada
the one goes into Toronto
bothered letters are stirred up out of order

explanation.surface: A Canadian headteacher shrugs off a stranger arriving in Toronto.
explanation.walkthrough: The Roman numeral goes into the city, then everything after Canada is stirred together; the capital C stays in front.
explanation.definitionFit: A contortionist twists their body, so is a twisted individual in a playful sense.

clue.text: Dreadful, like a doughnut filled with jam, ultimately

parts.note: à la, in the manner of

indicators.note: the doughnut has the letter put inside it

parts.note: a ring doughnut has a hole in the middle

indicators.note: the ultimate letter of jam is its last

explanation.surface: A jam doughnut is dreadful, apparently.
explanation.walkthrough: The jam is not the filling of a real doughnut: only its last letter, M, goes into RING.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both describe something that frightens or dismays.

clue.text: One of several hands, each forward

parts.note: a straight is one of the ranked hands in poker
a head, as in 'a pound a head'

explanation.surface: Several farmhands each step forward.
explanation.walkthrough: Hands suggests workers or body parts, but it means card hands.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for moving onward in the direction you face.

clue.text: Landlord perhaps wore pants into which name sewn

indicators.note: a name tape sewn into clothing sits inside it
pants is British slang for rubbish, so the letters of wore are rubbishly arranged

explanation.surface: A landlord wore underpants with his name stitched in.
explanation.walkthrough: Pants looks like underwear, which suits sewn-in name tapes, but it is British slang for rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: A landlord is an example of an owner, of the property he lets.

clue.text: Ruby cut fish

parts.note: ruby is a shade of red
a haircut, short at the front and long at the back

explanation.surface: A ruby is cut into the shape of a fish.
explanation.walkthrough: Cut looks like the jeweller's cutting of the ruby, but it is a haircut.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this reddish Mediterranean species is one fish among many.

clue.text: Figurine in op art, surprisingly a high price

indicators.note: the figurine goes in them
the letters of op art turn up in a surprising order

explanation.surface: An op art figurine unexpectedly sells for a lot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Surprisingly' works on op art alone; the figurine is then placed inside the result, splitting it.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for the most anyone will pay, money at the top of the scale.

clue.text: Rumba dancing country once

indicators.note: dancing letters move about into a new order

explanation.surface: People in some nation used to dance the rumba.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Once' makes the definition fair: Burma is now officially Myanmar.
explanation.definitionFit: Burma is the former name of Myanmar.

clue.text: Report in Religious Education yet to be handed in?

parts.note: homework not yet handed in is late

explanation.surface: A pupil's RE report hasn't been handed in yet.
explanation.walkthrough: Report looks like a noun, the school report, but it is the verb: to tell.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to report events is to tell or recount them.

clue.text: Powerless individual, male unfortunately with nothing

indicators.note: the male letters come out unfortunately jumbled

parts.note: a duck is a score of zero in cricket

explanation.surface: A weak man sadly ends up with nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: A duck is cricket's word for a batsman's score of nought.
explanation.definitionFit: A lame duck is a person, often an outgoing official, with no real power.

clue.text: Pig and tailless wild dog getting on

indicators.note: without its tail, the dog loses its last letter

explanation.surface: A pig and a stump-tailed wild dog are getting along together.
explanation.walkthrough: Getting on looks like getting along or ageing, but here it means climbing aboard.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the travel sense: passengers climbing aboard a bus or plane.

clue.text: Pal composed note, just like friends

indicators.note: the letters of pal are composed, set out afresh

parts.note: the tonic is the keynote of a scale

explanation.surface: A friend wrote a note saying you are just friends.
explanation.walkthrough: Composed and note suggest writing a letter, or music; only the second is right, and only for note.
explanation.definitionFit: A platonic relationship is close but not romantic, just like friends.

clue.text: I am on phone, still

explanation.surface: Someone says they're still on the phone.
explanation.walkthrough: Still reads as 'yet', but it is the adjective: not moving.
explanation.definitionFit: Still is the adjective here, not the adverb: motionless, unable to move.

clue.text: Mexican food: something sharp on it with last of tabasco

indicators.note: the last letter of tabasco

explanation.surface: Mexican food needs something hot poured on it, finished with Tabasco.
explanation.walkthrough: Something sharp suggests hot sauce, but it is a burr, the spiky seed head that catches on clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: A burrito is a Mexican dish of a tortilla wrapped round a filling.

clue.text: Journey heading for Florence, easy

indicators.note: the heading of Florence is its first letter

explanation.surface: A trip to Florence is straightforward.
explanation.walkthrough: Heading for looks like travelling to Florence, but it takes Florence's first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a trip taken by plane.

clue.text: Strike with wood cushioned by oaf

indicators.note: the wood is padded on both sides by the oaf

parts.note: the wood of the ash tree

explanation.surface: A clumsy lout hits someone with a wooden club.
explanation.walkthrough: Ash is a common crossword wood, and the oaf wraps around it, his first letter on one side and the rest on the other.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom meaning to hit out suddenly, as with a whip's lash.

clue.text: Arrive with something to smoke?

definitions.meaning: informal for turning up at a place

explanation.walkthrough: To roll up is to turn up; a roll-up is a hand-rolled cigarette, which the question mark flags as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Arrive in the informal sense of turning up; the second sense is a hand-made cigarette, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Lowest point in Florida now recalled

indicators.note: recalled letters are called back, read from the end
the answer sits in the words that follow

explanation.surface: Someone remembers the lowest point of their time in Florida.
explanation.walkthrough: Recalled looks like remembering, but it asks for the hidden letters backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: From astronomy, the point directly beneath the observer, used figuratively for the lowest point of anything.

clue.text: Irish premier, his ace reforms to follow universal principle

indicators.note: the rearranged letters come after the principle

parts.note: in Chinese philosophy, the Tao is the way underlying the universe

indicators.note: the letters of his ace are re-formed into a new order

explanation.surface: The Irish leader's star player reforms the country's founding principle.
explanation.walkthrough: Reforms reads as political change, fitting a premier, but it rearranges his ace.
explanation.definitionFit: The Taoiseach is the prime minister of Ireland.

clue.text: A part of a company, very skilful

explanation.surface: One division of a firm is highly competent.
explanation.walkthrough: DEPT is the usual abbreviation for department.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for highly proficient.

clue.text: In parts dry, Latino rum

parts.note: the French for dry, used of wine

indicators.note: rum means odd, so the letters of Latino are oddly arranged

explanation.surface: In some regions, Latin American rum is served neat.
explanation.walkthrough: Rum looks like the drink, apt beside dry, but it is the adjective meaning strange.
explanation.definitionFit: Built or divided into sections, which are parts.

clue.text: Dramatic performance observed in Europe rarely

indicators.note: the answer can be seen inside the next words

explanation.surface: A theatrical show is seldom seen in Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer spans the gap between the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: An opera is a dramatic work performed with music.

clue.text: First of challenges that hurt King Edward, say — lazybones!

indicators.note: the first letter of challenges

parts.note: what you say when something hurts
King Edward is a popular British variety of potato

explanation.surface: A monarch too idle to face his painful challenges.
explanation.walkthrough: King Edward suggests a monarch, but in Britain it is best known as a potato variety.
explanation.definitionFit: A couch potato is a lazy person who lounges in front of the TV.
